2. Historical Evolution of Clinical Reasoning: From the 1940s to
the Present
The history of clinical reasoning in the twentieth century reflects a fundamental transi-
tion from a practice based predominantly on authority, experience, and taxonomy toward a
formal science of decision-making. Until the mid-twentieth century, medical education was
strongly centered on the anatomoclinical model, which focused on recognizing syndromes,
localizing lesions, and correlating signs and symptoms with anatomical abnormalities.
While this paradigm provided a necessary foundation for diagnosis, it proved insufficient
for the probabilistic uncertainty and decision-making complexity that characterize modern
clinical practice [20].
Beginning in the 1940s and 1950s, three movements challenged it: clinical epidemi-
ology and medical statistics, which addressed uncertainty through sensitivity, specificity,
predictive values, and likelihood ratios; decision theory, which formalized weighing proba-
bilities against the benefits, harms, and costs; and the cognitive revolution investigated the
mental processes of problem solving [20].
The 1970s consolidated these emerging theories. Elstein, Shulman, and Sprafka pro-
posed the hypothetico-deductive model, in which clinicians generate early hypotheses and
then seek data to confirm, reject, or reformulate them [ 20]. Simultaneously, the work of
Tversky and Kahneman revealed that human judgment under uncertainty often relies on
heuristics, mental shortcuts such as availability, representativeness, and anchoring [21] and

legacy_cells.B: Clinical Reasoning, Pathophysiology, and Artificial Intelligence in Critical Care: A Conceptual Framework for Integrating Decision-Making
legacy_cells.C: Álvaro Réa-Neto; Jeane Cristina Fonseca Vieira
legacy_cells.I: 083_2026_Clinical Reasoning Pathophysiology and Artificial Intelligence in Critical Care A Conceptual Framework for Integrating Decision-Making.pdf
legacy_cells.EP: Proposed human-oversight measures: formulate an independent problem representation before consulting AI, request differential diagnoses, scrutinize pathophysiology, and keep final decisions with clinicians; not tested as an implemented system.
legacy_cells.EV: Proposed governance: local validation and calibration, model versioning, monitoring for performance drift after updates, audit trails, bias assessment, cybersecurity, privacy compliance, and incident reporting; no deployed lifecycle plan evaluated.
legacy_cells.FM: The authors' contribution is a conceptual synthesis integrating clinical reasoning, pathophysiology, and AI as a testable foundation for research and curriculum design, not a claim of demonstrated clinical benefit.
legacy_cells.FO: The authors report narrative-review selection by relevance judgment (possible selection bias), no formal risk-of-bias assessment or quantitative synthesis, an unvalidated conceptual framework, rapidly evolving AI evidence, and caution that much underlying literature comes from broader medical settings.
legacy_cells.FP: The authors call for prospective empirical validation of the integrative ICU framework; design and evaluation of reasoning-oriented AI; measurement of AI-induced cognitive biases; long-term evaluation of AI-integrated training; governance and safety standards; and learning-health-system integration.
legacy_cells.FQ: The authors identify a gap: clinical reasoning, pathophysiology, and AI have largely been treated separately, with few operational frameworks integrating Bayesian decision architecture, mechanistic coherence, and bedside AI governance.
legacy_cells.FR: Evidence boundary: this is a narrative/conceptual synthesis, not an implemented or empirically validated model or intervention. It reports no original evaluation demonstrating improved diagnostic accuracy, patient outcomes, or clinical safety; cited studies do not establish the proposed framework's effectiveness.
legacy_cells.FS: Reviewer mapping: M9 Safety & governance; M10 Clinician interface & lifecycle
legacy_cells.FT: Reviewer lesson: Carry the paper’s governance and evaluation considerations into a separate safety/lifecycle service; they do not validate a dynamics model.
legacy_cells.FU: Reviewer mapping (KB §20): Prospective evaluation & lifecycle governance
legacy_cells.FX: Complete extracted PDF text, pp. 1–21: title/abstract; introduction, search strategy and eligibility criteria; Sections 2–8; Tables 1–2 and figure captions; discussion and limitations; conclusions and future directions; author contributions, funding, IRB, data availability and acknowledgments; references and publisher disclaimer. | Codex audit: title/byline, abstract/conclusion, targeted methods/results and cross-check of prior quotations against extracted full text. This is a targeted audit, not an independent re-extraction of every negative/unreported field.
legacy_cells.FZ: A:I were preserved except B and C, which were corrected to match the PDF's printed title and two-author byline; E was filled from the journal header. The paper is a conceptual narrative review, not an implemented world model. Table 1's extracted layout has fragmented/misaligned columns; its contents were not used to assert original results. No original evaluation of the proposed framework is reported. Evidence QA: 13/16 populated fields had a <=25-word quotation matching extracted PDF text (81.2%).
